snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.subtitle: Aristotle's teacher, argued against here
snapshots.body: The chief target of Book II, where Aristotle works through the Republic's proposal that guardians hold wives, children and property in common, and the Laws' related scheme, and rejects both as impractical and as destroying the very variety that makes a state a state.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.subtitle: Plato's speaker in the Republic
snapshots.body: Cited throughout Book II as the voice who proposes, in Plato's Republic, that the guardian class hold everything — including women and children — in common for the sake of the city's unity. Aristotle argues the premise that more unity is always better is itself mistaken.

snapshots.name: Lycurgus
snapshots.subtitle: Legendary Spartan lawgiver
snapshots.body: The traditional author of the Spartan constitution, credited with the laws that shaped Lacedaemonian discipline, common meals and land arrangements. Aristotle treats him, alongside Solon, as a legislator whose actual constitution can be tested against theory.

snapshots.name: Solon
snapshots.subtitle: Athenian legislator
snapshots.body: The Athenian lawgiver who, among other reforms, prohibited any citizen from acquiring land beyond a set amount. Aristotle weighs his reputation as a good legislator against criticisms that his moderate settlement pleased no faction completely.

snapshots.name: Phaleas of Chalcedon
snapshots.subtitle: Theorist of property equality
snapshots.body: The first theorist, by Aristotle's account, to argue that citizens' landed properties should be made equal, on the reasoning that most political unrest is caused by disputes over property. Aristotle examines and largely rejects the scheme in Book II.

snapshots.name: Hippodamus of Miletus
snapshots.subtitle: City planner and constitutional theorist
snapshots.body: The son of Euryphon, credited as the inventor of the art of planned town layout and as the first person with no practical political experience to write about the best form of constitution, proposing a city of ten thousand citizens divided into three classes.

snapshots.name: Man, the Political Animal
snapshots.subtitle: Book I's founding claim
snapshots.body: Aristotle's foundational claim that the state exists by nature and that a human being is by nature meant to live in one — more fully a "political animal" than bees or any other gregarious creature, because only humans possess speech capable of expressing justice and injustice.

snapshots.name: The Best Form of Government
snapshots.subtitle: The work's long-run question
snapshots.body: The recurring inquiry, pursued through the surveys of existing and proposed constitutions in Books II–III and resumed in Books VII–VIII, into what arrangement of offices and citizens would actually produce the good life, as opposed to merely surviving or merely being praised in theory.

snapshots.name: The Causes of Revolution
snapshots.subtitle: How constitutions fail
snapshots.body: Book V's subject: the causes by which constitutions are overturned or corrupted from within, from disputes over property and honor to the ambitions of individual leaders — the diagnosis Aristotle offers for why even well-designed regimes tend to collapse.

snapshots.name: The Middle Class
snapshots.subtitle: Aristotle's stabilizing constituency
snapshots.body: The class of citizens with a moderate amount of property, neither very rich nor very poor, whom Aristotle repeatedly identifies as the most reliable foundation for a stable constitution, since a large middle class is least prone to the factional extremes that destroy states.
